results.title: Virtual lineages: in silico lineage tracing from single-cell and spatial transcriptomes
results.abstractText: Experimental lineage tracing reveals histories and fates of individual cells but is costly and often impractical, particularly in primary human tissues. Gene expression differences that persist across cell divisions provide a basis for inferring ancestry from more accessible single cell transcriptomes, yet accurate lineage reconstruction remains challenging. Here, we introduce isCORAL, an in silico lineage-tracing framework that reconstructs clonal relationships and maps cell-fate dynamics from transcriptome snapshots alone. By identifying memory genes with heritable expression differences, isCORAL infers probabilistic clonal relationships and uses them to construct clone-oriented embeddings and dynamic cell-fate maps. Across diverse lineage-tracing datasets, isCORAL markedly outperforms tested alternatives in both memory-gene identification and lineage reconstruction. We use isCORAL to resolve early fate biases among transcriptionally similar hematopoietic stem cells and predict distinct developmental routes to shared outcomes. We extend isCORAL to spatial transcriptomics, validating inferred clonal relationships against an experimentally recorded lineage tree in mouse tumors and inferring early epiblast and amnion dynamics in a human embryo. Together, isCORAL enables lineage-resolved studies of development and disease from standard single cell and spatial transcriptomes, and provides an explicit representation of lineage memory for future virtual cell models.

results.title: Industry updates from the field of stem cell research and regenerative medicine in August 2025
The influence of sensory function on walking stability in aging and falls through a head-movement perturbation model.
results.authorString: Lambrecht E, Embrechts E, Beckwée D, Vereeck L, Hallemans A, De Hertogh W.
results.abstractText: Age-related sensory decline impairs responses to balance disturbances, increasing fall risk. Evaluating gait and balance under sensory challenges can help reveal how this decline affects instability in older adults. This study (Clinicaltrials.gov NCT06345625) incorporates head movements to evaluate the effect of sensory function - cervical sensorimotor control, vestibular function, and visual acuity - on walking stability in aging and its relationship with falls through a novel augmented-reality perturbation model. Sixty-one healthy, community-dwelling older adults (76.2 years; 40 females) with and without fall history walked with head movements (up, down, left, right) cued by augmented-reality (marker-based motion capture and headset). Additionally, cervical sensorimotor control, vestibular semicircular canals (vestibulo-ocular reflex), and static visual acuity were tested. The effects of sensory functions on mediolateral and anteroposterior margin of stability and spatiotemporal parameters (step length, width, time and gait speed) were evaluated, including moderations of fall history through linear mixed models. Older adults with poorer cervical sensorimotor control and vestibular semicircular canal function increased cautiousness in their walking pattern during head movements through increasing step width, step time, and margin of stability. Worse visual acuity was associated with decreased walking stability. Sensory function was more strongly associated with walking stability in individuals with a history of falls. The effects of head movements on walking stability were associated with sensory functioning and falls in older adults. This highlights the potential of head movements as a functional perturbation for walking stability assessments linked with age-dependent sensory decline.

results.title: SubcellPert: Benchmarking Subcellular Perturbation Prediction
results.authorString: Wang J, Cao H, Dang X, Zhou T, Zhao Y, Hsieh C, Gu C, Heng PA.
results.abstractText: Perturbations change both RNA abundance and intracellular organization, but gene-count predictors omit the positions needed to model spatial responses. To address this limitation, we introduce \textbf{\textit{SubcellPert}}, a benchmark for perturbation-response prediction at single-RNA-molecule resolution. It comprises 14 imaging datasets with 13.88 million cells and 3.65 billion RNA molecules. Given source observations and a directed condition change, models generate target RNA populations in normalized two-dimensional coordinates. Two independently trained tasks separate abundance from localization: \textit{Oracle} predicts coordinates given exact target counts; \textit{Joint} predicts both. Eight baselines span source resampling, classical transport, and frozen foundation-model adapters. Fixed perturbation and cellular-context holdouts evaluate abundance error, target-gene coverage, and conditional spatial error. Through within-dataset analyses, we find context-dependent gains from spatial features in condition decoding. Interpreting spatial responses requires distinguishing changes within spatial clusters from population composition, and RNA fractions from enrichment relative to compartment geometry. Through comprehensive experiments, we find that Gaussian transport achieves the lowest Oracle spatial error on eight of eleven cellular-context OOD datasets. Audits show that better centroid accuracy can accompany worse radial distributions, and that 19 of 190 Joint adapter fits retain source counts after validation. SubcellPert opens a spatial frontier for virtual cell research, laying the groundwork for predictive models that capture both the molecular composition and intracellular organization of cellular responses. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/king159/SubcellPert}.

results.title: Generative inverse design steers human hematopoietic cell fate in vitro
results.authorString: Paulas-Condori L, Palma A, Consoli L, Rubio-Lara JA, Hidajat O, Zheng W, Klein D, Martinuzzi DG, Wu Z, Dittadi A, Wilson NK, Göttgens B, Theis FJ.
results.abstractText:
Summary

Inverse design has advanced the discovery of molecules and materials. Yet it remains largely unexplored for steering cell fate, where inputs are continuous, combinatorial culture conditions and outputs are distributions of cell states. Human hematopoiesis, in which combinations and doses of growth factors steer stem cells toward each blood lineage, is a demanding test case. While forward models can evaluate discrete conditions, the vast combinatorial space renders searching for a specific, target-producing design an intractable inverse problem. Here, we introduce LabCompass, an inverse-modeling framework that optimizes experimental designs toward candidates expected to produce specified target cell states, using a flow-matching generative model guided by cellular phenotypes predicted by a forward surrogate. We applied LabCompass to primary human CD34+ in vitro cultures, where continuous cytokine and small-molecule parameters govern hematopoietic cell fate. In a lab-in-the-loop setting, we experimentally validated model-driven designs and used these measurements to update the model across four successive loops. LabCompass recovered established lineage-inducing designs, improved predictions with new data, and enriched target populations across lineages. Incorporating new parameters expanded the design space and enriched rare populations beyond initial reach. Across loops, we generated a 78-million-cell spectral flow cytometry dataset and identified distinct culture conditions converging on the same target cell states. Our results establish generative inverse modeling as a compelling paradigm for navigating high-dimensional, continuous experimental spaces, and demonstrate that virtual cell models should be judged not only by how accurately they predict cellular responses, but also by how effectively they guide experiments toward desired biological outcomes.

results.title: Latent causal diffusions for single-cell perturbation modeling.
results.authorString: Lorch L, Zhang J, Bunne C, Krause A, Schölkopf B, Uhler C.
results.abstractText: Perturbation screens hold the potential to systematically map regulatory processes at single-cell resolution, yet modeling and predicting transcriptome-wide responses to perturbations remains a major computational challenge. Existing methods often underperform simple baselines, fail to disentangle measurement noise from biological signal, and provide limited insight into the causal structure governing cellular responses. Here, we present the latent causal diffusion (LCD), a generative model that frames single-cell gene expression as a stationary diffusion process observed under measurement noise. LCD outperforms established approaches in predicting the distributional shifts of unseen perturbation combinations in single-cell RNA-sequencing screens while simultaneously learning a mechanistic dynamical system of gene regulation. To interpret these learned dynamics, we develop an approach we call causal linearization via perturbation responses (CLIPR), which yields an approximation of the direct causal effects between all genes modeled by the diffusion. CLIPR provably identifies causal effects under a linear drift assumption and recovers causal structure in both simulated systems and a genome-wide perturbation screen, where it clusters genes into coherent functional modules and resolves causal relationships that standard differential expression analysis cannot. The LCD-CLIPR framework bridges generative modeling with causal inference to predict unseen perturbation effects and map the underlying regulatory mechanisms of the transcriptome.

results.title: Saccharopine and α-Aminoadipic Acid as Potential Biomarkers for Mitochondrial Stress in Neurons.
results.authorString: Ückert AK, Land A, Pape R, Alimohammadi M, Amelio I, Leist M.
results.abstractText: Redox stress and subsequent metabolic reprogramming are well-known consequences of neuronal exposure to mitochondrial toxicants. Here, we investigated, using human neuronal cultures, how such changes are quantitatively reflected in the patterns of cellular and extracellular amino acids. We asked whether these alterations may yield a mechanistically anchored biomarker for the type of neurotoxicity resulting from the impairment of the respiratory chain. Using a targeted metabolomics approach, we quantified intra- and extracellular amino acid pools and their temporal dynamics. Data were obtained from differentiated LUHMES neurons exposed to the complex I inhibitors berberine, 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP<sup>+</sup>), and tebufenpyrad, as well as to the non-mitochondrial toxicants MG-132 (proteasome inhibitor), RSL3 (glutathione peroxidase 4 inhibitor), and aerugine (fungal oxidative toxicant). The reductive stress, caused by mitochondrial inhibitors, was reflected in a characteristic and specific re-routing of amino acid metabolism, including increased Asn/Asp and Gln/Glu ratios and an upregulation of the electron acceptor Pro in neurons. Most conspicuous were the pronounced and reproducible increases in the lysine catabolites saccharopine (sacc) and α-aminoadipic acid (α-AAA). These two potential biomarkers of neuronal mitotoxicity were not altered by other types of toxicants. Moreover, the extent of concentration changes in sacc and α-AAA roughly correlated with the damaging effects of mitotoxicants, when assay conditions were (exposure period and exposure concentration). Our data provide an exemplary reference map of absolute amino acid concentrations in human cells and their culture medium. Moreover, sacch and α-AAA emerge as candidate biomarkers for neuroactive mitotoxicants and potentially for pathologies associated with impaired neuronal mitochondrial function.

results.title: Emerging frontiers for AI in single-cell genomics.
results.authorString: Mitra S, Li J, Leslie CS.
results.abstractText: We are just over a decade into the single-cell revolution in biology, which has been coupled to the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in single-cell genomics. Most early single-cell RNA embedding models and subsequent "foundation models"-representational models pretrained on large single-cell datasets-did not gain wide traction among experimental biologists. However, as massive single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlas efforts ramp up, there is a clear rationale for exploiting AI models to interpret new datasets in the context of vast existing data resources. Meanwhile, the advent of single-cell epigenetic/multiomic assays and Perturb-seq technologies presents new opportunities for AI modeling. Here, we review AI embedding and foundation models for scRNA-seq and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq), extensive machine-learning efforts to exploit single-cell multiome in regulatory genomics, and AI strategies to learn "virtual cell" models from Perturb-seq, ending with a description of current limitations of single-cell AI models and an outlook for future advances.

results.title: Process bigraphs and the architecture of compositional systems biology
The recoverable resolution of cellular perturbation-response prediction
results.authorString: Huang Y, Wang H, Li C, Wilson P.
results.abstractText: Virtual cell models aim to predict how cells respond to perturbations, yet accurate prediction of post-perturbation gene expression can conceal failures to recover context-specific responses. Here we identify context geometry compression (CGC), in which models preserve cellular identity and shared perturbation effects while collapsing differences in how the same perturbation acts across contexts. Across biological systems, reproducible context-specific responses remained difficult to recover; in a large drug-response matrix, this persisted even with nearly complete perturbation coverage. The same drug-response predictions achieved higher normalized recovery in predefined pathway summaries than in gene-level response profiles, while coarse response programs were more predictable in human lymphoblastoid cell lines. Compact baseline transcriptomic representations retained most full-RNA predictive performance for patient-specific ex vivo drug responses. Together, these findings establish recoverable biological resolution, rather than measurement dimensionality, as a criterion for evaluating virtual cell predictions and matching model outputs to the biological detail supported by evidence.

results.title: Post-Microbial Therapeutics for the Next Generation of Medicine.
results.abstractText: Post-microbial therapeutics is proposed here as an integrative, function-centered framework rather than a new therapeutic class. It asks whether a defined microbial perturbation can produce a reproducible change in a microbial function, biochemical output, and clinically relevant host phenotype. Bacteriophages provide a perturbation model because their host dependence permits strain-selective intervention, but the framework also distinguishes between whole phages and engineered phages, lysins, depolymerases, delivery systems, and combination products. A central requirement is that a microbial module must be defined by experimentally testable functional contribution rather than by statistical co-occurrence alone. Computationally inferred modules are therefore treated as hypotheses until supported by perturbation, reconstruction, removal/add-back, flux, or rescue experiments. Evidence reviewed across infection, gastrointestinal, biofilm, and cardiometabolic contexts shows a recurring pattern: phage exposure can alter bacterial abundance, resistance phenotypes, community interactions, and metabolism, but the strength of evidence diminishes as claims shift from bacterial killing to ecosystem restoration and host benefit. Engineering and delivery technologies can improve targeting or exposure, yet they introduce additional constraints in genetic stability, resistance, formulation, pharmacology, and regulation. The framework is consequently best viewed as a testable translational architecture that connects intervention to function and outcome while separating established evidence from emerging hypotheses.

results.title: scLDM: a conditional diffusion framework for single-cell perturbation prediction.
results.authorString: Wu B, Liu Y, Cheng Y, Liu X, Zou Q, Wei L, Xu L.
results.abstractText:
Motivation

Accurate prediction of single-cell responses to external stimuli is pivotal for deciphering gene regulatory mechanisms and accelerating data-driven drug discovery. However, effectively capturing the complex, non-linear mapping between intrinsic cell states and external stimuli remains an open problem.

Results

We propose scLDM, a generative framework based on latent diffusion models for predicting single-cell perturbation responses. scLDM first compresses high-dimensional gene expression into a compact latent space via a variational autoencoder, followed by a conditional diffusion process to generate post-perturbation states, explicitly guided by pre-perturbation cellular state, cell type, and perturbation type. Systematic evaluations on six datasets across diverse biological settings, spanning pharmacological stimulation, viral infection, helminth infection, genetic perturbations, and multi-species immune response contexts, demonstrate that scLDM achieves superior predictive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the model exhibits strong interpretability, as the learned perturbation embeddings show high functional alignment with known biological mechanisms. Overall, scLDM provides a robust and biologically consistent strategy for in silico perturbation screening.

Availability

The code is available at https://github.com/samrogers1233/scLDM and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22658164.
